medium.conteudo_html:
Setelah kupertimbangkan, aku pilih segelas es kopi buat nemenin ngerjain skripsi malam itu. Saat itu aku udah di tahun terakhir kuliah dan lagi pengen ngerjain skripsi di warmindo. Berisik tongkrongan mahasiswa terdengar dikiri kanan, sementara aku tenggelam di layar laptop dan catatan didepanku. Waktu itu, ChatGPT baru awal viral, tapi kemampuannya masih belum secanggih sekarang. Output-nya masih sering ngaco, jadi aku cuma pake buat ngerapihin kalimat doang, sementara urusan riset tetap kulakukan sendiri. Prosesnya berasa lambat banget. Mesti ngulik puluhan jurnal dan baca paper satu per satu cuma buat nyari referensi yang cocok. Belum lagi apesnya kalau dapet revisian dari dosen pembimbing. Capek, pusing, dan frustrasi paling pas buat ngegambarin kondisiku waktu itu. Bener-bener fase yang nguras banyak waktu dan tenaga.

Beberapa tahun kemudian setelah masuk dunia kerja, aku nyoba riset lagi buat keperluan brand. Kali ini aku nyoba pake ChatGPT lagi dengan asumsi kemampuannya udah jauh lebih jago. Benar aja, AI udah bisa bantu nyariin banyak sumber, ngerangkum puluhan paper, bahkan bisa sampe narik kesimpulan sendiri. Gilanya lagi, semua itu bisa kelar dalam hitungan detik. Kerjaan yang ngabisin waktu berjam-jam, sekarang bisa beres lebih cepat, gampang, dan efisien.

Tapi percaya nggak percaya, di tengah semua kegampangan itu aku justru ngerasa ada yang hilang. Emang sih, kerja tanpa dibantu teknologi (kayak AI) terasa lambat dan bikin puyeng. Tapi pas hampir semua prosesnya bisa dipercepat, ternyata ada momen berharga yang ikut hilang. Aku jadi kehilangan ruang buat melambat dan nikmatin serunya proses nyari jawaban yang bener-bener murni dari rasa penasaranku.

Terdengar aneh, tapi beneran itu yang kurasain. Pertanyaannya sekarang adalah:

Kenapa sesuatu yang super cepat dan efisien kayak AI justru bikin aku ngerasa kehilangan sesuatu? Apakah sebuah proses yang lambat sebenarnya punya keasikan sendiri? Atau emang udah saatnya kita ninggalin cara lama karena teknologi nawarin cara yang jauh lebih praktis?

Udah seberapa manja pake ChatGPT?

Ada eksperimen menarik yang ngelibatin 1.000 siswa SMA di Turki. Para peneliti ingin ngetes pengaruh AI buat efektifitas belajar matematika. Mereka membagi siswa jadi tiga kelompok:

  1. Kelompok ChatGPT Standar: Belajar pake AI yang langsung ngasih jawaban instan.
  2. Kelompok ChatGPT Tutor: Belajar pake AI yang disetting cuma buat ngasih clue dan feedback, bukan jawaban instan.
  3. Kelompok Non-AI: Belajar secara konvensional, cuma modal buku dan catatan kelas.

Pas lagi ngerjain tugas harian, hasilnya mungkin udah bisa kamu tebak. Kelompok ChatGPT Tutor dapet nilai paling tinggi, disusul kelompok ChatGPT Standar. Sementara itu, kelompok Non-AI dapat nilai paling jelek. Melihat hasil ini, gampang banget buat menyimpulkan kalo AI ternyata bisa meningkatkan performa siswa secara drastis.

Tapi, pas ujian tiba (yang nggak boleh pake AI sama sekali), hasilnya justru plot twist!. Kelompok ChatGPT Standar jatuh ke posisi paling bawah. Hal itu karena selama latihan, mereka terlalu bergantung sama AI. Kebiasaan disuapin jawaban instan bikin otak mereka lumpuh pas disuruh mikir mandiri. Sementara itu, kelompok ChatGPT Tutor sempet kepedean bakal dapat nilai tertinggi saat ujian setelah sebelumnya unggul selama tugas harian. Ternyata hasilnya malah diluar ekspetasi. Mereka nggak mampu ngalahin kelompok Non-AI secara mutlak. Selisih niainya-pun tipis banget, bahkan beberapa siswa yang belajar tanpa AI justru berhasil ngalahin mereka.

Siswa Non-AI emang dapat nilai paling jelek selama tugas harian. Tapi pas ujian tiba, hasil mereka justru melampaui ekspektasi. Padahal selama proses belajar, mereka yang berjuang paling berdarah-darah. Waktu ngerjain tugas harian, mereka nggak punya privilege berupa feedback instan pas lagi stuck. Prosesnya emang jauh lebih lambat dan nggak efisien. Tapi di balik itu semua, mereka justru mendapatkan satu privilege yang nggak dimiliki kelompok pengguna AI: ruang buat melambat dan bener-bener meresapi proses nyari jawaban dari rasa penasaran mereka sendiri. Pengalaman itulah yang nglatih mereka buat tetap bertahan saat nggak ada bantuan instan yang bisa diandelin ketika menghadapi sebuah masalah.

Katanya sih hidup itu harus sat-set

Kita sekarang hidup di zaman semuanya serba cepat. Dunia periklanan modern paham banget sama kelemahan psikologis kita yang satu ini. Makanya mereka pada berlomba-lomba menjual janji instan.

Tips sukses di usia 20-an, 100 juta pertama sebelum umur 30, tutorial menurunkan berat badan dalam seminggu.

Majunya teknologi makin bikin budaya instan ini mengakar kuat, dan artificial intelligence (AI) adalah wujud ekstremnya. Beberapa tahun ke depan, diprediksi bakal muncul Super AI (Artificial Superintelligence) yakni sebuah AI yang kecerdasannya jauh melampaui otak manusia. AI ini digadang-gadang sanggup mengambil alih hampir semua pekerjaan kognitif manusia yang paling rumit sekalipun. Dari sudut pandang produktivitas, ini jelas kabar bagus karena bisa memangkas tugas-tugas yang selama ini terasa lambat, ribet, dan memakan waktu. Sayangnya, hal ini justru bakal melahirkan satu masalah baru yang lumayan fatal: kita pelan-pelan mulai menganggap kalau semua proses yang lambat itu nggak berguna.

Padahal kalau kita benar-benar perhatikan, ada previlage dan manfaat tak tergantikan yang tersembunyi di balik sebuah “kelambatan”. Robert Bjork, seorang psikolog kognitif menyebutnya Desirable Difficulties. Konsep ini menjelaskan bahwa proses belajar yang terasa lebih sulit dan lambat justru bisa membuat kita mengingat dan memahami sesuatu jauh lebih baik.

Proses yang lambat dan berliku itulah yang sebenarnya memaksa otak kita berpikir kreatif saat stuck. Kelambatan ini memberikan kita ruang untuk merasakan pahitnya membuat kesalahan agar kemudian kita bisa belajar memperbaikinya. Pengalaman itulah yang perlahan melatih kita untuk jadi lebih disiplin dan tahan banting saat menghadapi kesulitan.

Google maps lovers, hati-hati ya!

Dulu sebelum ada GPS, kalau mau pergi ke tempat baru, kita terpaksa untuk mengingat nama jalan dan menghafal tiap belokan biar nggak nyasar. Memang terasa merepotkan. Lalu lahirlah teknologi bernama GPS. Tinggal ketik lokasi tujuan, ikuti arahan, dan sampe lah kita dilokasi. GPS jelas merupakan penemuan brilian yang menyulap urusan navigasi yang tadinya rumit jadi super praktis dan mudah.

Louisa Dahmani dan Véronique Bohbot, pernah menguji pengaruh ketergantungan GPS pada 50 pengemudi. Hasilnya, Orang-orang yang keseringan mengandalkan GPS ternyata punya spatial memory yang jauh lebih jelek pas ditantang nyari jalan sendiri secara mandiri. spatial memory ibarat GPS alami di dalam kepala kita. Ia adalah kemampuan otak buat ngerekam dan nginget tata letak lingkungan sekitar. Kemampuan inilah yang secara otomatis membentuk peta tak kasat mata di dalam kepala kita biar kita nggak gampang nyasar.

Using GPS removes these requirements and renders navigation less cognitively demanding. — Louisa Dahmani & Véronique D. Bohbot

Kita sering pakai teknologi buat menghindari proses yang terasa lambat dan merepotkan. Padahal, justru dibalik proses yang merepotkan itulah ada manfaat yang jauh lebih besar dari yang kita kira.

Mau sukses kok takut gagal?

Salah satu alasan kenapa kita begitu terobsesi dengan hal-hal instan itu karena kita terlalu fokus pada hasil akhir. Sadar atau nggak, kita hidup di tengah masyarakat yang lebih menghargai pencapaian. Kita ngasih standing ovation buat atlet yang berhasil meraih medali emas, tapi sering nutup mata sama ribuan jam latihan berdarah-darah yang sudah mereka lalui. Nggak ada ceritanya tetangga bakal ngasih apresiasi pas kita lagi sibuk berproses dan gagal.

Maka kita perlu tahu bahwa semuanya ini bukan cuma tentang hasil akhir. Saat kita lagi memecahkan sebuah masalah, ada dua produk yang sedang kita ciptakan.

  1. Pertama, produk berupa ‘jawaban’ atau hasil akhir itu sendiri.
  2. Kedua, produk berupa kemampuan kognitif yang kebentuk selama kita mikir dan berproses.

AI memang jago banget buat menghasilkan produk pertama. Tapi, kalo kita nggak berhati-hati, kita akan menjadi ketergantungan dan bakal kehilangan kesempatan buat membangun produk kedua. Di sinilah letak keajaiban dari sebuah proses yang lambat.

Studi dari MIT meminta 54 peserta menulis esai. Mereka dibagi dua kelompok: satu pakai bantuan AI, dan satu lagi menulis secara manual. Peserta yang dibantu AI jelas bisa nyelesaiin esainya jauh lebih gampang. Tapi, data menunjukkan kalo peserta dari kelompok AI ini ternyata punya pemahaman yang jauh lebih dangkal. Mereka juga kesulitan pas disuruh ngejelasin ulang esai mereka sendiri.

Makannya kenapa sih kita nggak boleh terlalu terobsesi pada hasil akhir? Karena pada proses yang lambat itulah yang benar-benar membentuk skill dan kapasitas kita.

You learn nothing from success. You learn everything from failure. — Ed Sheeran.

Semua pencapaian yang kita raih itu aslinya adalah hadiah dari keberanian kita menahan rasa capek dan sabar melewati proses yang panjang. Sayangnya, budaya serba instan ini seolah mencuci otak kita, membuat kita merasa kalau proses yang lambat itu adalah tanda ketertinggalann.

Padahal, sama sekali nggak ada yang sia-sia dari sebuah proses yang lambat. Kemunduran dan kegagalan bukan hal yang memalukan. Justru di fase-fase berat itulah, kapasitas diri kita lagi benar-benar ditempa buat naik ke level yang jauh lebih baik.

No AI? Siapa takut!

Di dunia yang serba cepat ini, kemampuan buat melambat dan nikmati proses itu jadi sesuatu yang langka. Makannya, belakangan ini aku mulai membiasakan satu hal sederhana: sesekali, coba bermain tanpa AI. Tujuanku bukan sengaja buat mempersulit hidup. Aku cuma pengen memberi ruang buat diriku sendiri untuk memakai ketrampilan yang kini perlahan mulai digantikan oleh teknologi.

Misalnya pas bikin template jurnal. Daripada langsung nyuruh AI membuatkannya, aku nyoba membuatnya sendiri. Banyak coretan dan selalu trial & eror. Tapi dari proses yang ribet itulah, akhirnya aku nemuin template yang paling cocok untuk diriku sendiri.

Austin Kleon, penulis buku Steal Like an Artist, punya kebiasaan yang menarik. Dia sengaja membagi ruang kerjanya jadi dua meja: analog desk dan digital desk. Analog desk cuma boleh ada kertas, pena, pensil, spidol, dan koran. Semua perangkat elektronik kayak komputer dan scanner disingkirin kedigital desk. Analog desk memberi ruang bebas bermain pakai tangan dan isi kepala kita sendiri tanpa distraksi dari digital world. Ada ruang untuk bereksperimen dan membuat karya sebebas-bebasnya.

This is where most of my work is born . — Kleon tentang analog desk-nya.

AI memang menawarkan sesuatu yang cepat dan efisien. Tapi dalam hidup, ketidakefisienan dalam berproses itulah yang justru paling kita butuhin buat terus bertumbuh. Itulah mengapa kita tetep wajib belajar matematika dasar, meskipun udah ada kalkulator. Tujan kita bukan sekedar bisa menghafal rumus, tapi karena kemampuan itulah yang pada akhirnya membentuk fondasi berpikir kita sebagai manusia.

Say goodbye to AI, tapi bentar…

Gerakan “Say No to AI” jadi salah satu kampanye yang rame di internet. Wajar saja, terutama bagi para pekerja kreatif yang merasa posisinya terancam. Namun, akar masalahnya sebenarnya lebih dalam. AI sering dilatih dengan cara menyedot miliaran data dan karya berhak cipta tanpa izin. Eksploitasi data ini jelas melanggar etika, dan aku pun sepenuhnya mendukung perlawanan terhadap kelakuan perusahaan-perusahaan raksasa tersebut.

Sayangnya, sebagian orang menjadi terlalu fanatik sampai menolak AI secara membabi buta. Mereka enggan beradaptasi dan terus dirongrong kecemasan. Padahal, disrupsi macam ini bukan hal yang baru. Saat Revolusi Industri terjadi, banyak pekerja yang juga merasa kiamat sudah dekat gara-gara munculnya mesin pabrik. Kabar baiknya, sejarah sudah membuktikan kalau manusia punya kemampuan adaptasi yang luar biasa. Menutup mata dari keberadaan AI justru hanya akan merugikan diri sendiri, karena teknologi akan terus berkembang. Hukum alam di dunia modern selalu sama: adapt or you will be defeated.

Kelompok siswa yang pakai ChatGPT Standar nilainya hancur lebur saat ujian, sementara mereka yang pakai ChatGPT Tutor masih mampu bersaing dengan siswa Non-AI. Ini jadi bukti kalo masalahnya bukan terletak pada keberadaan AI itu sendiri, melainkan bagaimana kita memanfaatkannya.

Suka nggak suka, dunia modern akan menjadikan AI sebagai bagian dari kehidupan kita. Setelah paham bahwa alat ini bisa membuat kita tumpul jika dipakai sembarangan, maka mindset kitalah yang harus diubah. Jangan jadikan AI sebagai mesin pencetak jawaban instan, jadikanlah ia rekan diskusi. Tetaplah pro-aktif dan kritis terhadap apa pun output yang diberikan AI. Jadikan AI sebagai alat, lalu smua keputusan tetap berada ditangamu. Pada akhirnya, mungkin bukan AI yang akan menggantikan peran kita, tetapi mereka yang tahu cara memanfaatkan AI dengan lebih baik.

Buat yang Lebih Suka Baca ChatGPT Ketimbang Baca Buku

Apakah kamu termasuk orang yang kalo punya pertanyaan langsung refleks buka ChatGPT ketimbang mencari jawabannya di buku? Memang jauh lebih cepat dan efisien. Tapi ternyata, manfaat membaca buku bukan cuma soal dapat pengetahuan baru. Ketika membaca pelan-pelan, tanpa sadar kita juga sedang melatih banyak hal:

  1. Menandai kalimat penting melatih kita mengidentifikasi poin-poin krusial.
  2. Menulis argumen di pinggir buku melatih kita untuk berpikir kritis.
  3. Mencoba memahami cara berpikir dan sudut pandang penulis melatih kita melihat sesuatu dari perspektif yang berbeda.
  4. Menulis kesimpulan dengan bahasa sendiri melatih kita menyederhanakan ide yang rumit sekaligus menghubungkan berbagai informasi yang sebelumnya terasa terpisah (connecting the dots).

Nah, kayak yang udah berkali-kali aku bilang, di balik proses yang lambat tuh, selalu ada manfaat besar yang tersembunyi.

Namun jujur, sampai sekarang akupun masih pakai ChatGPT buat bantu nyelesaiin beberapa masalah. Tapi belakangan, aku mulai sengaja buat nggak selalu bergantung dengannya. aku mulai sadar, ngga semua proses yang lambat perlu kita tinggalkan cuma gara-gara teknologi menawarkan cara yang lebih efisien.

Mengerjakan sesuatu sendiri memang terasa lambat dan merepotkan. Tapi, justru di situlah aku menemukan ruang untuk melambat mencari jawaban yang lahir dari rasa penasaranku sendiri. Melambat bukan berarti kita tertinggal, karena dari situlah aku belajar rasanya menikmati sebuah proses.

Thank you for reading!

Sources & References

Bastani et al. (2025) — Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. PNAS. Study involving nearly 1,000 students in Turkey.

Robert A. Bjork & Elizabeth L. Bjork (2020) — Desirable Difficulties in Theory and Practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition.

Dahmani, L. & Bohbot, V. D. (2020) — Habitual use of GPS negatively impacts spatial memory during self-guided navigation. Scientific Reports.

Kosmyna et al. (2025) — Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task. MIT Media Lab.

Austin Kleon — Steal Like an Artist. The “Analog Desk” and “Digital Desk” concept.

Ed Sheeran (2023) — Interview with Howard Stern. “You learn nothing from success. Nothing. You learn everything from failure.”

Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) — General references on hypothetical AI systems that could surpass human cognitive abilities.

The Industrial Revolution & the Luddites — Historical references on technological disruption, automation, and workers adapting to new technologies.

medium.titulo: I Stopped Building MCP Servers for Everything. Here’s What I Use Instead
medium.resumo: How Claude plugins turned a week of server work into an afternoon of markdown.
medium.conteudo_html:
How Claude plugins turned a week of server work into an afternoon of markdown.

A few months ago, I needed Claude to answer questions about orders in our backend system. Simple ask: “What’s the status of order 4521? Why is it stuck?”

My reflex was to build an MCP server. So I did. I spun up a .NET project with the MCP SDK, defined a GetOrderStatus tool with its input schema, wrote the handler that called our orders API, set up the transport, figured out auth, and deployed it. Then I wrote a README explaining to my team how to configure their clients to connect.

It worked. It also took far longer than the problem deserved, and the first question anyone asked was “why does it say Pending Reconciliation, what does that mean?” The tool could fetch the status. It had no idea what the status meant.

That’s when I started looking seriously at Claude plugins.

The shift: from code that routes to context that guides

The core building block of a plugin is a skill. Here’s roughly what my order lookup became:

orders-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── skills/
    └── order-lookup/
        ├── SKILL.md
        └── scripts/
            └── get_order.sh

And the SKILL.md:

markdown

---
name: order-lookup
description: Use when the user asks about an order's status,
  why an order is delayed, or what an order state means.
---
# Order Lookup
To fetch an order, run `scripts/get_order.sh <orderId>`.
## What the statuses mean
- **Pending Reconciliation**: payment received but not yet matched
  to an invoice. Usually resolves within 24 hours. If older than
  48 hours, tell the user to contact finance.
- **On Hold**: flagged by inventory. Check the `holdReason` field.
...

That’s the whole thing. The script hits the same endpoint my MCP handler did. But now the business knowledge (what the statuses mean, what to do about them) sits right next to the action. Claude doesn’t just fetch the order; it explains it.

Why it feels so much lighter

The first thing I noticed was context efficiency. With my MCP setup, tool definitions sat in context from the start of every conversation. With skills, Claude only sees the name and description until the skill becomes relevant. Then it loads the full instructions. I can ship twenty skills and they cost almost nothing until someone needs one.

The second thing was iteration speed. When finance told me the 48-hour threshold should be 72, I changed one line of markdown and pushed. No rebuild, no redeploy.

The deployment moment

This is where I actually laughed out loud.

To share the plugin, I added a marketplace.json to a .claude-plugin folder at the repo root, listing the plugin. Pushed the repo. That repo is now a marketplace.

My teammates ran:

/plugin marketplace add our-org/claude-plugins
/plugin install orders-plugin@our-org

Done. No server URL, no config walkthrough, no “it works on my machine.” When I update the plugin, I push to the repo. We’ve since added plugins for our deployment workflow and our SQL conventions, and new engineers get our entire AI toolkit in a couple of commands.

What I didn’t throw away

I want to be honest here, because a lot of posts oversell this. I didn’t delete every MCP server.

For integrations that need a persistent authenticated connection, or that other AI clients also use, MCP is still the right tool. And plugins can bundle MCP server configs, so I now ship those servers inside plugins, alongside skills that teach Claude how to use them properly.

The change is in my default. It used to be “build a server.” Now it’s “write a skill, and build a server only if the skill genuinely can’t do the job.” Most of the time, it can.

Try this

Pick the one internal system your team asks Claude about most. Write a single SKILL.md that explains how it works and includes one script that calls it. Put it in a repo with a marketplace manifest and install it.

It’ll take you an afternoon. It took me a week the other way.

medium.titulo: Claude Pro vs Max vs API: What the Plans Actually Cost a Heavy User
medium.resumo: Anthropic sells Claude in multipliers and the API in tokens. Converted into one unit: where Pro, Max 5x and Max 20x stop being the cheap…
medium.conteudo_html:
Anthropic sells Claude in multipliers and the API in tokens. Converted into one unit: where Pro, Max 5x and Max 20x stop being the cheap option.

Anthropic sells Claude by the multiplier. Pro gives you “at least 5x more usage per 5-hour session than Free”; Max is “5x or 20x more usage per 5-hour session than Pro”. Nowhere does a plan page tell you how many messages that is, and Anthropic says so plainly — there is no fixed message count, because length and complexity decide how much of the window a request eats.

The API sells the same model by the token. So the two things you are choosing between are not quoted in the same unit, and the usual advice — “just get Max if you use it a lot” — is a guess dressed as a rule. OpenAI creates the same comparison problem; our ChatGPT Plus vs Pro vs API analysis prices its current tiers with the same method.

This converts one into the other. Every figure below was computed with the same functions that run the calculators on this site, against published rates.

What the plans cost

  • Free — Monthly: $0 · What it says you get: “Free covers everyday questions”
  • Pro — Monthly: $20 ($17 billed annually, $200 upfront) · What it says you get: “at least 5x more usage per 5-hour session than Free”
  • Max 5x — Monthly: $100 · What it says you get: “5x more usage per session than the Pro plan”
  • Max 20x — Monthly: $200 · What it says you get: “20 times more usage per session than the Pro plan”

Two details matter more than the prices. Limits reset on a rolling five-hour session, with weekly limits on top. And usage is shared across every surface — claude.ai, the desktop app and Claude Code all draw from the same allowance, so “I only use Claude Code” is not a separate budget. If Claude Code is the main thing you run, the fairer comparison is with the other coding agents — we price Claude Code against Cursor and Codex task by task.

The API has no session window and no weekly cap. It has a bill.

The crossing point, on a chat-shaped request

Start with the easy case: a question of about 700 tokens in and a 900-token answer — a normal exchange, not a document.

Where each plan stops being the cheap option

Claude Sonnet 5, a 700-token question and a 900-token answer, no caching.

  • Pro — Per month: $20 · Break-even: 1,923 · ≈ per working day: 87 questions
  • Max 5x — Per month: $100 · Break-even: 9,615 · ≈ per working day: 437 questions
  • Max 20x — Per month: $200 · Break-even: 19,231 · ≈ per working day: 874 questions

Source: CalculatorAI subscription-vs-API engine · rates verified 2026–09–09

One such request costs $0.0104 on the API. So Pro pays for itself at roughly 1,900 questions a month, and Max 20x needs about 19,000 — call it 874 a working day, which is a question every thirty-three seconds for eight hours.

If that were the whole story, almost nobody should be on Max. It is not the whole story, and the reason is the shape of the requests, not their number.

Real requests are not chat-shaped

A coding turn is not 700 tokens of input. It carries files, a system prompt, tool definitions and the conversation so far — 18,000 tokens of input against a 1,200-token reply is conservative for an editing session.

  • Chat question — One request: $0.0104 · Pro: 1,923/mo · Max 5x: 9,615/mo · Max 20x: 19,231/mo
  • Coding turn — One request: $0.0480 · Pro: 417/mo · Max 5x: 2,083/mo · Max 20x: 4,167/mo
  • Coding turn, 90% cached — One request: $0.0188 · Pro: 1,062/mo · Max 5x: 5,308/mo · Max 20x: 10,616/mo

The same plan buys a quarter as many coding turns as chat questions. Pro’s break-even falls from 1,923 requests to 417 — about nineteen a working day, which any real session passes before lunch.

Note also what caching does to that row: it more than doubles the break-even, from 417 to 1,062. On the API, caching the fixed part of a request is billed at roughly a tenth of the base input rate, and it moves the line further than upgrading a plan does.

So is the API cheaper? For single turns, dramatically

Take someone who would describe themselves as a heavy user, on the cached coding shape, twenty-two working days:

  • 20 — Sonnet 5 on the API: $8.29 · Opus 5 on the API: $20.72
  • 60 — Sonnet 5 on the API: $24.87 · Opus 5 on the API: $62.17
  • 150 — Sonnet 5 on the API: $62.17 · Opus 5 on the API: $155.43

A hundred and fifty coding turns a working day is a lot of work, and on Sonnet it is $62 against $200 for Max 20x. Even on Opus it stays under the plan price.

This is the number people quote when they say the API is cheaper. It is correct, and it is measuring the wrong thing.

The agent loop is where it reverses

A coding “turn” is rarely one call. Ask an agent to do something and it reads, edits, runs, reads the failure and edits again — and each step resends the conversation so far, so input grows roughly with the square of the number of steps. Same model, same caching, twenty tasks a working day:

One task, or a loop: the same month on the API

20 agent tasks a working day, system prompt cached, no retries.

  • Claude Sonnet 5–6 steps per task: 36 → 14 steps per task: 146 $ a month
  • Claude Opus 5–6 steps per task: 90 → 14 steps per task: 364 $ a month
At fourteen steps on Opus the API costs more than Max 20x — the plan is the cheap option.

Source: CalculatorAI agent-cost engine · rates verified 2026–09–09

A single call is $4.93 a month. Six steps a task is $35.95. Fourteen steps is $145.70 — nearly thirty times the one-call figure for work a user would describe identically. On Opus the same fourteen-step loop is $364.24 a month, comfortably past Max 20x.

That inversion is the answer to the question in the title. The API is cheaper for people who send requests. The subscription is cheaper for people who start loops.

Expressed as a daily allowance, on Sonnet with an eight-step loop:

  • Pro, $20 — Agent tasks a working day before the API costs more: ~10
  • Max 5x, $100 — Agent tasks a working day before the API costs more: ~49
  • Max 20x, $200 — Agent tasks a working day before the API costs more: ~98

Ten agent tasks a day is a normal Tuesday. Ninety-eight is not.

Caching beats upgrading

Before changing plan in either direction, price the caching. Same eight-step loop, twenty tasks a day, Sonnet:

  • None — Per task: $0.1180 · Per month: $71.78
  • System prompt and tools cached — Per task: $0.0928 · Per month: $56.45
  • Conversation cached too — Per task: $0.0531 · Per month: $32.31

Caching the conversation cuts the bill by 55% — more than the difference between two plan tiers, and it changes nothing about the answers. If your agent carries tool definitions from MCP servers, that overhead is its own line item and it is larger than most people expect.

Seats are the part people forget

A subscription is per person. An API key is shared. Five people doing forty cached coding turns a day each:

  • Five Max 5x seats — Monthly: $500.00
  • The same work on the API — Monthly: $82.90

That gap is not a rounding error, and it grows linearly with the team. It is also the case where the comparison is least honest about what you lose: five people on the API need something to type into, and the plan includes that.

What I would actually do

  • If your usage is conversational, the API wins and it is not close. Pro needs about 87 questions a working day to pay for itself.
  • If you run agents, buy the plan. Ten agent tasks a day already passes Pro; a heavy Opus loop passes Max 20x. Price the loop rather than the request — the AI Agent Cost Calculator models growing context, retries and caching per call.
  • Turn on caching before you change anything. 55% on the same work, same model, same output.
  • Count seats before you compare. One API key against five subscriptions is a different question from one against one.
  • Then check your own numbers, not these. Put your real request sizes into the subscription vs API calculator — it prints the crossing point and how far your current volume sits from it, which is the only figure that decides anything.

One honest caveat, and it is not a small one: this compares price and nothing else. A plan buys an interface, a mobile app, file uploads and a support relationship; an API key buys tokens. On the API side alone, how Anthropic’s per-task prices compare with OpenAI’s and Google’s is in our ChatGPT vs Claude vs Gemini cost comparison. If the interface is how you work, the cheaper column is not automatically the right one.

Where these numbers come from

Plan prices and the wording of the limits are Anthropic’s own, from the pricing page and the Max plan help article, read on 11 September 2026. CalculatorAI is not affiliated with Anthropic.

Every dollar figure is ours, computed by importing the same functions that run the calculators on this site, against Anthropic’s published API rates as verified on the date shown on each calculator page. The assumptions:

  • Claude Sonnet 5 at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output; Claude Opus 5 at $5 and $25. Cached input is billed at a tenth of the base input rate.
  • The chat shape is 700 input tokens and 900 output. The coding shape is 18,000 input and 1,200 output, which is a mid-session edit rather than a first message.
  • Agent rows use a 2,000-token system prompt, a 300-token instruction, 350 tokens written per step, 600 tokens returned per tool call, and a context that grows with every step.
  • 22 working days a month. No batch discount.
  • No retries anywhere. A real agent fails calls, re-reads files and makes a second attempt at a bad plan, so every agent figure here is a floor, not a forecast.

Where the assumptions bias the result: the single-turn rows flatter the API, because they price a request rather than the loop a person actually starts. The agent rows flatter the subscription slightly less than reality would, because retries are excluded. And token counts outside OpenAI’s tokenizer are estimates with a stated range — Claude’s exact count is not something any calculator can know, ours included.

Related reading

The four numbers that decide any AI bill — the model, the resent prompt, the loop and the length of the answer — are worked through in what AI actually costs once you run it. If your agent has MCP servers attached, their tool definitions ride along on every step and cost more than most people’s model usage. And if Claude arrives on your card as a monthly plan rather than a bill, it belongs in a subscription audit with everything else that renews quietly.

medium.titulo: Introducing Nuxt Native v1 — Developer Preview
medium.resumo: Build truly native mobile apps with Vue and the Nuxt developer experience, powered by NativeScript.
medium.conteudo_html:
Build truly native mobile apps with Vue and the Nuxt developer experience, powered by NativeScript.

Today, we’re introducing the developer preview of Nuxt Native — an open-source framework for building native mobile applications using Vue and familiar Nuxt conventions.

If you already love building with Nuxt, Nuxt Native aims to make mobile development feel familiar too.

Instead of rendering your application inside a WebView, Nuxt Native uses NativeScript to render real native UI on Android and iOS.

With Nuxt Native, we’re bringing familiar ideas from the Nuxt ecosystem to native development:

  • Vue Single File Components
  • File-based routing
  • Nuxt-style composables
  • Native UI components
  • Pinia support
  • Native device APIs
  • Simple CLI and developer tooling

This is just the beginning.

Repo:

https://github.com/vastx-tech/nuxt-native

Nuxt Native is currently in Developer Preview, and there is still a lot to build, improve, and explore. We’re releasing early so developers can try it, experiment with it, contribute, and help shape its future.

Our goal is simple:

Make native mobile development feel natural for Vue and Nuxt developers.

Welcome to Nuxt Native. 🚀

medium.titulo: SPA (React/Vue) vs. htmx: Why Towami Chose a Document-First Frontend
medium.resumo: A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.
medium.conteudo_html:
A marketplace page should arrive as usable HTML — for search engines, modern laptops, and mid-range phones on mobile networks.

React and Vue are excellent tools. We chose a different architecture for Towami’s public catalog and merchant storefronts because of the product’s requirements, not because JavaScript frameworks are inherently slow or bad for SEO.

Where React and Vue are the right choice

When the product is primarily an application — a design tool, trading terminal, collaborative editor, or state-heavy dashboard — a component framework and client runtime are often the most productive choice.

The ecosystems are mature, the development model is widely understood, and frameworks such as Next.js and Nuxt can return fully rendered HTML from the server. A React or Vue application is not automatically a client-only SPA, nor is it automatically bad for search.

Shopify illustrates why the distinction matters. Its standard theme stack is an excellent default for many merchants, with mature commerce tooling and broad app compatibility. Shopify Markets supports localized languages, currencies, pricing, and domains. For teams that need a custom headless storefront and already work in React, Hydrogen is also a strong option.

Those are rational choices. Towami’s requirements simply led to a different trade-off.

The boundary we have

Towami has two closely connected public surfaces:

  • country marketplaces across nine markets, with localized English and Spanish routes;
  • white-label merchant storefronts, including storefronts on merchants’ own domains.

Organic search is an important acquisition channel. That means some filter combinations are more than temporary UI state: when they have live inventory, they become indexable landing pages.

For example:

https://cr.towami.com/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

That URL needs to return a complete document with a canonical URL, structured data, localized metadata, and — when the combination is eligible — a sitemap entry. It should not exist only after a client-side router has started.

A client-heavy architecture could meet those requirements. But it would add another layer that must remain consistent with the server: routes, locales, currencies, canonical rules, cache variants, and the initial document received by crawlers.

We decided that Towami did not need that layer on its public surfaces.

What the browser receives

Towami’s public UI is rendered by Go using Templ templates.

Browser-side behavior uses htmx, Alpine.js, and a project-specific JavaScript bundle:

  • htmx requests and replaces HTML fragments;
  • Alpine manages local state such as mobile menus, confirmation dialogs, galleries, and checkout options;
  • the site bundle handles behavior that does not fit cleanly into either library.

Navigation is boosted at the <body> level. Ordinary internal links can replace #main-content and update browser history without replacing the entire document. The header remains mounted, with out-of-band updates where its content needs to change.

The initial catalog content arrives as server-rendered HTML. There is no React or Vue hydration step. After an htmx update, Alpine initializes behavior on the new DOM.

Critical CSS for public pages is inlined, while the remaining styles are loaded from separate bundles. Account pages use linked stylesheets because their first render is not an organic-search landing surface.

The largest browser-side dependency is TipTap. It is loaded only in merchant content editors — for products, pages, blog posts, and categories — not in the public catalog.

One URL, two navigation modes

Catalog filters are where this architecture becomes especially useful.

Suppose a visitor selects “sedan.” The filter form uses GET.

For an htmx request, the server:

  1. returns 200 OK;
  2. renders the catalog fragment;
  3. sends HX-Push-Url with the preferred path.

The list updates and the address bar becomes:

/en/vehicles/cars/for-sale/sedan

For an ordinary request — including a browser without JavaScript — the same query-string URL receives a 302 redirect to the preferred path.

There is no crawler detection. The server only distinguishes an htmx request from a regular HTTP request.

Canonical URLs remove non-SEO filters such as price ranges. One allowlisted feature can become the final path segment; additional features remain in ?features=. Sitemap generation only publishes combinations supported by live catalog data.

This gives enhanced navigation to browsers that support it while keeping the underlying links and forms functional without JavaScript.

Keeping response variants separate

A full document and an htmx fragment can share a URL while containing different HTML. The cache must not confuse them.

Towami’s primary full-page and htmx navigation responses use a weak ETag calculated from the rendered body and return:

Vary: Accept, HX-Request, X-Catalog-More
Cache-Control: private, no-cache, must-revalidate

Because the full document, navigation fragment, and “show more” fragment have different bodies, they receive different ETags. A matching conditional request returns 304 Not Modified.

We do not attach a public millisecond claim to this mechanism. The relevant architectural property is simpler: the first response contains the page, while enhanced navigation uses the same URL model instead of creating a second client-only route space.

What we gave up

This approach has costs.

We gave up the standardized React/Vue client-component ecosystem, shared frontend language across server and browser, and the tooling built around large client-side applications.

The merchant interface is also server-rendered. Initial requests return complete Templ pages; subsequent navigation can replace #main-content with htmx fragments. A server-backed interaction usually means implementing a handler that returns markup rather than designing a JSON API and client store.

That model is less attractive for dense interfaces with extensive client state.

We also do not try to turn every transition into app-style navigation. Authentication links and several other flows deliberately perform normal document navigation. Progressive enhancement is a default, not a requirement that every request must be asynchronous.

When we would choose React or Vue

We would choose a client framework if Towami’s primary interface became a real-time operations console, visual page builder, collaborative editor, or another product where most meaningful state lives in the browser.

That would justify the runtime and client-side state model. The public catalog and merchant storefront could still remain document-first.

Modern React and Vue frameworks can also reduce client cost through server components, selective hydration, lazy hydration, and hybrid rendering. The trade-off is therefore one of degree, not an absolute limitation of those technologies.

For Towami, the remaining client-side requirements were small enough that adopting a full application runtime for every public page did not provide enough value.

Performance is a target, not a slogan

Core Web Vitals are among the signals used by Google’s ranking systems, although good scores do not guarantee rankings. Across ecommerce, faster experiences often correlate with better conversion — but that is something each product should measure, not promise in advance.

Towami’s engineering target is a high PageSpeed score and good Core Web Vitals on merchant storefronts. It is not an unconditional guarantee for every page or every uploaded image.

The architecture makes that target more achievable:

  • compiled server-side templates;
  • usable HTML in the initial response;
  • inlined critical CSS;
  • limited JavaScript on public pages;
  • no application-framework hydration;
  • one URL model for visitors and crawlers.

React and Vue remain excellent choices for products that behave primarily as applications. Towami’s public catalog is document-first, with interactivity added where it provides clear value.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Douglas Cerqueira, organizador da Maratona de Salvador, revela novidades sobre a prova, incluindo novo percurso e arena. Ele também detalha os planos para a nova Maratona da Bahia, focada na cultura local, e a importância do Circuito Brasil Gigante. E mais: a resposta do quiz…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 27 de setembro de 2026

Em uma entrevista exclusiva gravada durante o TS Summit, Douglas Cerqueira, da MP3 Live Marketing, organizador da Maratona de Salvador, compartilhou detalhes sobre o evento deste ano e os planos para o futuro. Com a expectativa de reunir entre 10 e 11 mil pessoas, a prova está a quatro semanas de acontecer e passa por ajustes finais.

Uma das principais novidades é uma mudança no percurso. Devido a obras na cidade, a arena do evento foi realocada para dentro do Centro de Convenções de Salvador, oferecendo uma estrutura melhor para os atletas. Apesar disso, o percurso da maratona continua sendo 100% na orla.

Douglas também falou sobre o crescimento da prova, que faz parte de um plano estratégico para torná-la um evento de destaque nacional e, futuramente, internacional. A corrida já possui o selo Ouro da CBAt e o selo da World Athletics, o que eleva o nível de exigência em diversos aspectos, como a estrutura médica, que agora conta com UTI e segue as novas diretrizes da confederação.

Além da Maratona de Salvador, que faz parte do Circuito Brasil Gigante, um novo projeto está a caminho: a Maratona da Bahia. Prevista para o primeiro semestre do próximo ano, a prova será realizada em parceria com a RG+ e terá como objetivo resgatar o protagonismo da Cidade Baixa de Salvador. O percurso passará por pontos turísticos icônicos, com largada próxima ao Elevador Lacerda e ao Mercado Modelo, e integrará um grande evento cultural para mostrar a riqueza das manifestações da Bahia.

Quiz Musical: quem inventou o trio elétrico?

A resposta para o quiz do dia é uma dupla que marcou a história do carnaval baiano. Os criadores do trio elétrico foram Dodô e Osmar, que levaram a invenção às ruas de Salvador pela primeira vez no carnaval de 1950.
